questions.q: Three people check into a hotel room costing $30, splitting it $10 each. The manager realizes the room was only $25 and sends the bellhop back with $5. The bellhop, unable to split $5 three ways, gives each guest $1 back and pockets $2. Each guest has now paid $9, totaling $27, plus the bellhop's $2 makes $29. Where did the missing dollar go?
choices: The math is correct and a dollar truly vanished
Nowhere — the $27 already includes the bellhop's $2, so adding them double-counts; $27 paid = $25 room + $2 pocketed

questions.q: A biologist says: 'Every one of my lab's rats that drank the experimental compound survived. Therefore the compound is safe.' What is the most glaring logical flaw, assuming the lab also ran rats that did NOT drink it?
choices: There is no flaw — the conclusion follows directly
The claim ignores whether the untreated control rats also survived at the same or higher rate
Rats are not a valid model for any biological claim
The sample size of rats is always too small to matter

You flip a fair coin four times. Which is more likely: the coin landing on HHHH (four heads in a row), or on HTHT (heads, tails, heads, tails)?
choices: Neither is possible with a fair coin
They are equally likely (each has probability 1/16)

questions.q: In 1995, David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter. In 1996, Justice again had a higher average than Jeter. Yet combining both years together, Jeter's overall average was higher than Justice's. Is this mathematically possible?
choices: Yes — this is a real, documented case (Simpson's paradox)
This could only happen due to a scorekeeping error
No — if Justice led in both years he must lead overall
No — batting averages are strictly additive across years

questions.q: In the St. Petersburg game, a fair coin is flipped until it lands tails; if the first tails occurs on flip n, the payout is $2ⁿ (so $2 if tails on flip 1, $4 on flip 2, and so on). What is this game's expected value?

You have 12 identical-looking coins. Exactly one is counterfeit and weighs slightly differently from the rest (you don't know if it's heavier or lighter). Using a balance scale, what is the minimum number of weighings needed to guarantee finding the counterfeit coin?

Three guests pay $30 for a room ($10 each). The manager sends back $5 via the bellboy, who keeps $2 and gives $1 to each guest. Each guest paid $9 (total $27); add the bellboy's $2 and you get $29. Where is the missing dollar?
choices: There is no missing dollar — the bellboy's $2 is already part of the $27 paid, not additional to it
The hotel manager kept an extra dollar by mistake
One guest was overcharged by a dollar
